# Sima de los Huesos hominins
Sima de los Huesos hominins refers to a population of Middle Pleistocene human ancestors discovered at the Sima de los Huesos (“Pit of Bones”) site in the Sierra de Atapuerca, northern Spain. The remains date to approximately 430,000 years ago and comprise at least 28 individuals from a single population. This makes Sima de los Huesos the largest and one of the oldest known collections of hominin fossils ever found at one site. These hominins are characterized as early Neanderthals or “proto-Neanderthals” – they exhibit a mosaic of Neanderthal-like anatomical features in the face, teeth, and jaws, combined with more primitive traits in the braincase. Genetic evidence has confirmed that the Sima de los Huesos people belonged to the Neanderthal lineage, although their mitochondrial DNA shows an unexpected link to the Denisovans of Asia. The site’s remarkable fossil assemblage has provided key insights into the evolution of Neanderthals and has sparked debate over how and why so many bodies came to rest at the bottom of a deep cave shaft.
## Discovery and Site
Sima de los Huesos is a deep chamber within the Cueva Mayor–Cueva del Silo cave system of the Atapuerca Mountains in Burgos Province, Spain. The chamber lies about 30 meters underground, at the base of a vertical shaft approximately 13 meters (43 ft) deep and only a few meters wide. Access to this “Pit of Bones” is difficult and requires descending the narrow chimney-like shaft from an upper cave passage. The site is part of the larger Sierra de Atapuerca UNESCO World Heritage area, known for rich paleoanthropological finds spanning over a million years of human prehistory.
Systematic excavations at Sima de los Huesos began in 1984 under Spanish paleoanthropologist Juan Luis Arsuaga and colleagues. Over the ensuing decades, researchers recovered thousands of fossil bones from the chamber. Due to the cave’s depth and narrow access, excavations are challenging: archaeologists must haul sediment and fossils up the shaft in difficult conditions. Nevertheless, the site has yielded an unprecedented trove of hominin remains as well as animal fossils. The first human bones were found in the 1980s, but major discoveries continued into the 1990s and 2000s as teams expanded the excavation. By the 2010s, Sima de los Huesos had produced more identifiable human fossils than any other single Paleolithic site in the world.
## Fossil Assemblage
The Sima de los Huesos deposit contains more than 6,500 hominin bone fragments representing at least 28 individuals, alongside a large accumulation of animal remains. The human fossils include skulls, jaws, teeth, and virtually all major bones of the body, often broken and scattered but exceptionally well-preserved by the cave sediments. Notably, parts of about 17 distinct skulls have been recovered, several of them nearly complete. The individuals include both males and females and an age range from adolescents to mature adults (roughly At least one nearly complete pelvis and numerous vertebrae, limb bones, and hand/foot bones have also been found, allowing researchers to reconstruct body size and anatomy in detail.
In addition to the human fossils, the bone layer contained remains of many carnivorous animals. Fossil bones of cave bears (Ursus deningeri) are especially abundant – over 160 bear individuals are estimated at the site. Other carnivores found include extinct species of lions, wildcats, wolves, foxes, and lynx. Unlike typical predator den sites, however, the Sima de los Huesos assemblage has a curious absence of herbivore prey animals. Most of the hominin and animal bones were not found in natural articulation, and some show gnaw marks from scavengers, indicating that carnivores did chew on a few of the corpses. However, detailed taphonomic studies found that only about 4% of the bones (human or animal) have tooth marks, suggesting the cave was not primarily a carnivore lair or feeding site.
One striking aspect of the assemblage is the presence of a single stone tool amid the thousands of bones. This lone artifact is a finely made hand axe of red quartzite, nicknamed “Excalibur.” It was found near the human remains and is of Acheulean typology (Mode 2). No other stone tools, debris, or signs of habitation were recovered in the pit. The uniqueness of the Excalibur hand axe – in raw material and quality – and its isolated context have led to speculation that it may have been a deliberate offering or grave good, possibly the world’s oldest-known funerary offering. This interpretation remains conjectural but highlights the unusual context of Sima de los Huesos as more than a typical living site.
## Anatomy and Classification
The human fossils from Sima de los Huesos exhibit a combination of anatomical traits that position them on the evolutionary line leading to Neanderthals. They are often described as “proto-Neanderthals” or early members of the Neanderthal lineage. For example, the faces show pronounced mid-facial projection and double-arched brow ridges, similar to classic Neanderthals. The jawbones and teeth are robust: the mandibles are thick with retromolar spaces, and the anterior teeth show heavy wear, suggesting use of teeth as tools – a known Neanderthal behavior. Dental studies have found that Sima dentition has inner enamel and dentine patterns virtually identical to later Neanderthals, reinforcing their close relationship. In contrast, other parts of the skeleton retain more primitive features. The cranial vaults (braincases) are shaped more like earlier humans, with somewhat smaller brain capacity. The average cranial volume of the Sima hominins is around 1,230 cubic centimeters, which is slightly below that of later Neanderthals (∼1,410 cc) and modern humans (∼1,350 cc). Postcranially, they were short and stocky: estimates suggest males stood about 1.70 m tall and weighed around 77 kg (170 lbs), while females were roughly 1.58 m and 57 kg (125 lbs). This body build aligns with the cold-adapted, robust physique associated with Neanderthals, even though these individuals lived during a temperate phase between glacial periods.
When the first Sima de los Huesos fossils were studied in the 1990s, researchers initially classified them as Homo heidelbergensis, a broad species category for mid-Pleistocene humans in Europe. H. heidelbergensis was named for a roughly 600,000-year-old jaw from Germany and was thought to be a likely ancestor of Neanderthals. The Atapuerca team initially “lumped” the Sima remains into this species due to some primitive characteristics and their intermediate age. However, as more bones were recovered, distinctive Neanderthal-like traits became clear. In 2014, Juan Luis Arsuaga and colleagues published an influential study examining 17 skulls from Sima de los Huesos, and concluded that these fossils did not fit within H. heidelbergensis. The Sima hominins showed many derived features shared with Neanderthals (especially in the face, jaw, and teeth) that were absent in H. heidelbergensis fossils from elsewhere. At the same time, they differed from other known fossils of similar age (such as those from Ceprano and Arago in Europe) and from later “classic” Neanderthals. Because of this unique combination, Arsuaga’s team suggested that the Sima population might warrant designation as a new species, or at least a separate population within the Neanderthal lineage. As of the mid-2020s, no new species name has been formally assigned – the Sima de los Huesos hominins are generally considered early Neanderthals in a broad sense, occupying a position just before the fully developed Neanderthal form of the later Ice Age.
Paleoanthropologists describe the pattern of traits in the Sima fossils as evidence of mosaic evolution. That is, different anatomical features evolved at different rates: key Neanderthal characteristics in the dental and facial region appeared early (by 430,000 years ago), while other features like an enlarged brain and very robust body form evolved later. The Sima skull study found that the face, teeth, and jaw show a suite of Neanderthal-derived adaptations likely related to intensive biting and chewing (for example, using front teeth as a “third hand”). In contrast, the smaller braincase and certain limb bone features remained more primitive. This supports the idea that Neanderthal ancestors gradually accrued their distinctive anatomy piecemeal, rather than all at once. The Sima de los Huesos population, living roughly midway between the time of H. erectus and classic Neanderthals, provides a rare snapshot of this evolutionary process in action.
## Genetic Evidence
Sima de los Huesos is notable for yielding the oldest hominin DNA yet recovered. The cool, sealed cave sediments helped preserve genetic material for nearly half a million years. In 2013, researchers managed to extract and sequence mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) from a hominin thigh bone found in the pit. The results were surprising: the mtDNA did not match what was expected for a Neanderthal ancestor. Instead, the Sima mtDNA showed a closer affinity to the mtDNA of the Denisovans – an extinct human lineage known from Asia – even though the Sima hominins’ skeletal features clearly align with Neanderthals. This unexpected finding suggested a complex scenario in which the mitochondrial lineage in these European hominins might have originated from an ancestral population common to Denisovans, or was later replaced in Neanderthals by gene flow from another group.
Subsequently, in 2016, scientists from the Max Planck Institute reported the sequencing of nuclear DNA from Sima de los Huesos fossils, including fragments of the genome from a femur and a tooth. Although the recovered nuclear DNA comprised only about 0.1% of the full genome, it was sufficient to establish evolutionary relationships. The nuclear DNA conclusively showed that the Sima de los Huesos individuals were early Neanderthals, genetically closer to later Neanderthals than to Denisovans or modern humans. In other words, despite the Denisovan-like mtDNA, the overall genome places them on the Neanderthal branch after the split from the modern human lineage. These fossils lived around the time that the Neanderthal and Denisovan lineages were diverging from each other, which might explain the mixed signal. One hypothesis is that the Sima de los Huesos hominins initially carried an ancestral mtDNA lineage (common to Denisovans), and that Neanderthals subsequently acquired a different mitochondrial lineage later—perhaps through interbreeding with an African population that migrated into Europe. This scenario would reconcile the genetic data with the anatomy, indicating the Sima population are indeed Neanderthal ancestors with an archaic mtDNA signature.
The success of DNA recovery from Sima de los Huesos was a breakthrough for paleogenetics. At roughly 430,000 years old, these are by far the oldest hominin DNA sequences ever obtained, eclipsing the next-oldest (Neanderthal DNA from ~120,000-year-old specimens) by over 300,000 years. The achievement required advanced techniques to retrieve highly fragmented, degraded DNA from non-permafrost bones. The findings have provided direct genetic confirmation of the evolutionary hypothesis that the Sima de los Huesos group falls on the Neanderthal lineage. They also highlight that our picture of hominin relationships can be complex – for example, the unexpected Denisovan link hints at previously unknown population interactions in the Middle Pleistocene. Ongoing research on ancient DNA from Sima de los Huesos and other sites may further clarify how Neanderthals, Denisovans, and modern humans each inherited different pieces of their ancestry.
## Deposition and Possible Mortuary Practices
Why the remains of so many hominins (along with numerous carnivores) accumulated in a remote cave chamber is one of the most debated aspects of Sima de los Huesos. Several hypotheses have been proposed, and the true circumstances may never be fully known. The traditional explanation is that the Sima was a natural trap: humans and animals could have fallen down the vertical shaft in sporadic events over time, dying upon impact or being unable to escape the deep pit. According to this scenario, the shaft functioned like a death trap or natural pitfall. This would be analogous to other fossil sites (such as natural sinkholes or caves) where animal bones accumulate after accidental falls. The geology of the site – a steep shaft leading to a sloping “ramp” and chamber – is consistent with a natural drop into the pit. Supporting this, many of the Sima bones were found in a mud-breccia matrix with evidence of mudflows, which could have helped transport or mix the bones after deposition. The presence of so many cave bear remains in the same pit strongly suggests that animals were routinely tumbling into the hole over centuries. Bears likely fell during hibernation explorations, as evidenced by scratch marks on the shaft walls from trapped bears clawing to escape. By this view, the human individuals might also have entered the pit by accidental falls or even been washed in during flood events.
However, certain aspects of the Sima de los Huesos assemblage are difficult to explain with a purely accidental scenario. One observation is that all the hominin fossils appear to be of a similar age (roughly 430,000 years) and potentially deposited around the same time, rather than representing many separate incidents over tens of thousands of years. Moreover, the demographic profile of the humans is non-random: studies of the remains indicate an overrepresentation of adolescents and young adults, with fewer very young or old individuals than might be expected in a natural death sample. Out of the ~28 individuals, only one was under about 10 years old and none were elderly; most were in their teen or adult prime years. If the cave were simply a long-term trap or cemetery, one might expect a broader range of ages including more children, since child mortality was high in prehistory. The relatively selective age distribution hints that the assemblage might not result from random accidents alone.
Another hypothesis suggests periodic carnivore activity: perhaps large carnivores (like cave bears or hyenas) dragged human corpses into the cave. Yet this is not strongly supported by the evidence. As noted, there are few bite or gnaw marks on the human bones, and crucially, no remains of common prey herbivores were found that would indicate a den where carnivores fed regularly. It appears unlikely that any predator specialized in hunting humans to bring into the cave. The absence of herbivore bones (deer, bovids, etc.) and the deep location argue against the cave being a regular carnivore den.
The most provocative interpretation – advocated by the lead excavators – is that Sima de los Huesos represents an intentional disposal of the dead by other humans, essentially a form of mortuary behavior. Juan Luis Arsuaga and some colleagues propose that the 28 individuals did not arrive by chance, but were deliberately dropped or deposited in the pit after death. This would make the site the oldest known example of funerary practice or body disposal by hominins. The idea is supported by the lack of habitation debris and the singular hand axe Excalibur possibly serving as a ritual offering. Proponents note that deliberate body disposal would neatly explain why so many individuals of one group ended up together, and why their bones are largely of similar age and condition. It could represent a social practice where this cave shaft was used as a place to lay the dead – a kind of natural tomb.
Skeptics of the mortuary hypothesis caution that it is difficult to prove intent in the deep past. They argue that natural processes could still account for much of the evidence: for instance, a catastrophic event or disease could have killed many members of a group whose bodies later found their way into the shaft via flooding or earth movements. Yet, some physical evidence does hint at foul play or intentionality. One skull (specimen Cranium 17) from Sima de los Huesos was found to have two penetrating fractures on the forehead, injuries that forensic analysis indicates were likely caused by blows from a blunt object. The two wounds are similar in size and shape, suggesting repeated intentional trauma rather than an accidental fall. This 2015 analysis (by Nohemi Sala and colleagues) argued that the individual died from these injuries – potentially making it one of the earliest identified cases of homicide in human history. Furthermore, the study contends that the presence of a murder victim in the assemblage is consistent with bodies being intentionally cast into the pit (whether by perpetrators hiding their crime, or by a group ritually disposing of their dead). If humans were indeed disposing of bodies in the shaft – whether as a form of simple corpse removal or as a ritualistic act – it would push back the origins of mortuary practices to a remarkably early date, over 200,000 years before the earliest widely accepted burials.
In sum, the deposition of the Sima de los Huesos hominins remains an open question. Current evidence has made some scenarios (like a long-term carnivore den) unlikely, while lending some support to the idea of deliberate accumulation. The “Pit of Bones” may have been a natural trap that multiple humans and animals fell into, possibly exacerbated by occasional flooding that swept in remains. Alternatively, it might represent a planned disposal site used by these early humans to place their deceased. Both perspectives find some backing in the site data, and they are not mutually exclusive (for example, a deliberate disposal could have occurred in a pit that was already known as a dangerous natural trap). Ongoing excavations (as much of the deposit is still unexcavated) and further analyses may provide more clues. Whatever the case, Sima de los Huesos offers an extraordinary glimpse into the lives—and deaths—of a Middle Pleistocene human community.
## Significance
The discovery of the Sima de los Huesos hominins has been hugely significant for paleoanthropology. It provides an unparalleled collection of fossils from a single population of archaic humans, allowing scientists to study variation and development within a group 430,000 years ago. The site has yielded insights into the anatomical evolution leading toward Neanderthals, showing which traits appeared early and which came later in the lineage (supporting the idea of modular, regional evolution of Neanderthal features). Because the fossils are so well-preserved and numerous, researchers have been able to examine growth patterns, calculate demographic profiles, and even diagnose pathologies or injuries on these ancient humans, building a detailed picture of their biology and lifeways.
Sima de los Huesos also anchors the timeline of human evolution in Europe. The precise dating of the deposit (~430 ka, achieved by multiple techniques) makes these the oldest known hominins clearly on the Neanderthal lineage. This helps calibrate molecular clocks and evolutionary scenarios, confirming that the Neanderthal branch and the modern human branch had already split by this time. The genetic evidence from Sima further illuminates this period, hinting at population dynamics (like possible interbreeding events or population replacements) in the mid-Pleistocene that were previously only conjectured. In particular, the unexpected Denisovan link from the mtDNA has spurred new hypotheses about how widespread and interconnected populations were across Eurasia at that time.
Finally, the Sima de los Huesos site has raised provocative questions about the cognitive and cultural capabilities of early humans. If the accumulation of bodies was indeed intentional, it suggests that hominins hundreds of thousands of years ago may have had concepts of death, group identity, or ritual far earlier than assumed. Even if the mortuary interpretation is not conclusively proven, the very consideration of it expands the discussion of cognitive archaeology into much deeper time. The possible murder evidence from Cranium 17 likewise provides a window into social behavior (and conflict) in these ancient communities. In essence, Sima de los Huesos is not just a trove of bones, but a rich source of information about the morphology, genetics, and behavior of our distant relatives. Ongoing research at this site continues to refine our understanding of where the Sima people fit in the human family tree and how they lived and died in the deep past.

This would be analogous to other fossil sites (such as natural sinkholes or caves) where animal bones accumulate after accidental falls.
The geology of the site – a steep shaft leading to a sloping “ramp” and chamber – is consistent with a natural drop into the pit.
Many of the Sima bones were found in a mud-breccia matrix with evidence of mudflows.
Mudflows could have helped transport or mix the bones after deposition.
The presence of so many cave bear remains in the same pit strongly suggests that animals were routinely tumbling into the hole over centuries.
Bears likely fell during hibernation explorations, as evidenced by scratch marks on the shaft walls from trapped bears clawing to escape.
By this view, the human individuals might also have entered the pit by accidental falls or even been washed in during flood events.
However, certain aspects of the Sima de los Huesos assemblage are difficult to explain with a purely accidental scenario.
One observation is that all the hominin fossils appear to be of a similar age (roughly 430,000 years) and potentially deposited around the same time.
The hominin fossils at Sima de los Huesos do not represent many separate incidents over tens of thousands of years.
The demographic profile of the humans at Sima de los Huesos is non-random.
Studies of the remains indicate an overrepresentation of adolescents and young adults, with fewer very young or old individuals than might be expected in a natural death sample.
Out of the ~28 individuals, only one was under about 10 years old and none were elderly.
Most of the individuals were in their teen or adult prime years.
If the cave were simply a long-term trap or cemetery, one might expect a broader range of ages including more children.
Child mortality was high in prehistory.
The relatively selective age distribution hints that the assemblage might not result from random accidents alone.
Another hypothesis suggests periodic carnivore activity: perhaps large carnivores (like cave bears or hyenas) dragged human corpses into the cave.
The hypothesis of periodic carnivore activity is not strongly supported by the evidence.
There are few bite or gnaw marks on the human bones from Sima de los Huesos.
Crucially, no remains of common prey herbivores were found that would indicate a den where carnivores fed regularly.
It appears unlikely that any predator specialized in hunting humans to bring into the Sima de los Huesos cave.
The absence of herbivore bones (deer, bovids, etc.) and the deep location argue against the Sima de los Huesos cave being a regular carnivore den.

The most provocative interpretation – advocated by the lead excavators – is that Sima de los Huesos represents an intentional disposal of the dead by other humans, essentially a form of mortuary behavior.
Juan Luis Arsuaga and some colleagues propose that the 28 individuals did not arrive by chance, but were deliberately dropped or deposited in the pit after death.
This would make the Sima de los Huesos site the oldest known example of funerary practice or body disposal by hominins.
The idea of intentional disposal is supported by the lack of habitation debris and the singular hand axe Excalibur possibly serving as a ritual offering.
Proponents note that deliberate body disposal would neatly explain why so many individuals of one group ended up together.
Deliberate body disposal would explain why the bones are largely of similar age and condition.
It could represent a social practice where this cave shaft was used as a place to lay the dead – a kind of natural tomb.
Skeptics of the mortuary hypothesis caution that it is difficult to prove intent in the deep past.
Skeptics argue that natural processes could still account for much of the evidence.
A catastrophic event or disease could have killed many members of a group whose bodies later found their way into the shaft via flooding or earth movements.
Some physical evidence does hint at foul play or intentionality at Sima de los Huesos.
One skull (specimen Cranium 17) from Sima de los Huesos was found to have two penetrating fractures on the forehead.
Forensic analysis indicates that the injuries on Cranium 17 were likely caused by blows from a blunt object.
The two wounds on Cranium 17 are similar in size and shape, suggesting repeated intentional trauma rather than an accidental fall.
This 2015 analysis (by Nohemi Sala and colleagues) argued that the individual died from these injuries.
The death of the individual from Cranium 17 potentially makes it one of the earliest identified cases of homicide in human history.
The study contends that the presence of a murder victim in the assemblage is consistent with bodies being intentionally cast into the pit.
Bodies might have been cast into the pit by perpetrators hiding their crime, or by a group ritually disposing of their dead.

If humans were indeed disposing of bodies in the shaft – whether as a form of simple corpse removal or as a ritualistic act – it would push back the origins of mortuary practices to a remarkably early date.
The origins of mortuary practices would be pushed back over 200,000 years before the earliest widely accepted burials.
The deposition of the Sima de los Huesos hominins remains an open question.
Current evidence has made some scenarios (like a long-term carnivore den) unlikely.
Current evidence lends some support to the idea of deliberate accumulation at Sima de los Huesos.
The “Pit of Bones” may have been a natural trap that multiple humans and animals fell into.
The natural trap scenario could possibly be exacerbated by occasional flooding that swept in remains.
Alternatively, Sima de los Huesos might represent a planned disposal site used by these early humans to place their deceased.
Both perspectives find some backing in the Sima de los Huesos site data.
The perspectives on Sima de los Huesos are not mutually exclusive.
A deliberate disposal could have occurred in a pit that was already known as a dangerous natural trap.
Ongoing excavations (as much of the deposit is still unexcavated) and further analyses may provide more clues about Sima de los Huesos.
Sima de los Huesos offers an extraordinary glimpse into the lives—and deaths—of a Middle Pleistocene human community.
The discovery of the Sima de los Huesos hominins has been hugely significant for paleoanthropology.
Sima de los Huesos provides an unparalleled collection of fossils from a single population of archaic humans.
The Sima de los Huesos collection allows scientists to study variation and development within a group 430,000 years ago.
The Sima de los Huesos site has yielded insights into the anatomical evolution leading toward Neanderthals.
Sima de los Huesos shows which traits appeared early and which came later in the Neanderthal lineage.
The Sima de los Huesos findings support the idea of modular, regional evolution of Neanderthal features.

Because the Sima de los Huesos fossils are so well-preserved and numerous, researchers have been able to examine growth patterns, calculate demographic profiles, and even diagnose pathologies or injuries on these ancient humans.
The Sima de los Huesos fossils build a detailed picture of the biology and lifeways of these ancient humans.
Sima de los Huesos also anchors the timeline of human evolution in Europe.
The precise dating of the Sima de los Huesos deposit (~430 ka, achieved by multiple techniques) makes these the oldest known hominins clearly on the Neanderthal lineage.
This helps calibrate molecular clocks and evolutionary scenarios.
The Sima de los Huesos findings confirm that the Neanderthal branch and the modern human branch had already split by this time.
The genetic evidence from Sima further illuminates this period.
The genetic evidence from Sima hints at population dynamics (like possible interbreeding events or population replacements) in the mid-Pleistocene that were previously only conjectured.
In particular, the unexpected Denisovan link from the mtDNA has spurred new hypotheses about how widespread and interconnected populations were across Eurasia at that time.
The Sima de los Huesos site has raised provocative questions about the cognitive and cultural capabilities of early humans.
If the accumulation of bodies was indeed intentional, it suggests that hominins hundreds of thousands of years ago may have had concepts of death, group identity, or ritual far earlier than assumed.
Even if the mortuary interpretation is not conclusively proven, the very consideration of it expands the discussion of cognitive archaeology into much deeper time.
The possible murder evidence from Cranium 17 provides a window into social behavior (and conflict) in these ancient communities.
Sima de los Huesos is not just a trove of bones, but a rich source of information about the morphology, genetics, and behavior of our distant relatives.
Ongoing research at Sima de los Huesos continues to refine our understanding of where the Sima people fit in the human family tree.
Ongoing research at Sima de los Huesos continues to refine our understanding of how the Sima people lived and died in the deep past.

Prehistoric bones found in Spain are ancestors of Neanderthals
==============================================================

This article is more than 11 years old

Discovery suggests distinctive Neanderthal features evolved at different rates

[Joel Achenbach](https://www.theguardian.com/profile/joel-achenbach)

Tue 1 Jul 2014 14.00 BST

[Share](mailto:?subject=PrehistoricbonesfoundinSpainareancestorsofNeanderthals&body=https://www.theguardian.com/global/2014/jul/01/features?CMP=share_btn_url)

In a cave in northern Spain a team of scientists has retrieved the remains of 28 prehistoric humans, members of an enigmatic species that could be described as a little bit Neanderthal.They had Neanderthal faces, with heavy brows and protruding noses. They had powerful mandibles and mouths that could open extremely wide, indicating they used their teeth as gripping tools. But they didn't have the large skulls or other robust skeletal features seen in the prototypical [Neanderthals](https://www.theguardian.com/science/neanderthals) who, hundreds of millennia later, roamed Ice Age Europe.

These were apparently ancestors of Neanderthals, inhabitants of a line that many thousands of years earlier had split from the ancestors of modern humans. An international team of scientists published the description of the Spanish fossils in the journal [Science](http://www.sciencemag.org/), but has not yet given this population a new species name. That will come later, the scientists said, after consultations with colleagues.

The discovery does not dramatically change the general picture of human evolution, but it complicates it a bit, providing new evidence that there were many distinct, and largely isolated, human species existing simultaneously, and competing with one another in a harsh environment marked by advancing and retreating ice sheets.

The lead author of the new paper, paleoanthropologist Juan Luis Arsuaga of the [Universidad Complutense de Madrid](https://www.ucm.es/english), refers to this as "a [Game of Thrones](http://www.hbo.com/game-of-thrones) scenario".

As he put it, there was no Middle Pleistocene kingdom ruling over everything, but rather many competing houses vying for the same land.

"Hominin evolution was not a peaceful, boring process of very slow change over time," Arsuaga said.

The fossil site, in a cave called Sima de los Huesos ("Pit of Bones"), is in a chamber at the bottom of a vertical shaft. Arsuaga believes it was a mortuary – a repository for the dead. There are also many fossilised bones of bears, and claw marks on the wall. The bears may have become trapped in the pit.

Archeologists have bones but not much else to work with – there are no cultural artifacts in the pit other than a single hand axe.

The first bones were first found at the Sima site many years ago, and Arsuaga and his colleagues originally lumped them together with another early human species called [_Homo heidelbergensis_](http://humanorigins.si.edu/evidence/human-fossils/species/homo-heidelbergensis). But the new analysis, which includes the description of 17 skulls, concludes that these early humans were physically distinct from their heidelbergensis contemporaries.

"This is a big advance. I'm sorry that it's still sort of swinging out there in taxonomic limbo instead of having been given its own designation," said [Ian Tattersall](http://www.amnh.org/our-research/staff-directory/ian-tattersall), a paleoanthropologist at the American Museum of Natural History, who was not involved in the new research.

Arsuaga and his colleagues believe the fossils show that the Neanderthals lineage did not get all its distinctive anatomical features as a complete set, but rather these appeared individually, in "a mosaic pattern of evolution, with different anatomical and functional modules evolving at different rates", in the words of the Science paper.

The scientists suggest that the evolution of the Neanderthal lineage is tied to an adaptive trait associated with chewing. Although the paper in Science does not speculate about what drove the evolution of specialised features for chewing, Arsuaga said he believes these Neanderthal ancestors could have used their teeth to grip meat or other objects.

"We could speculate that Neanderthals had three grasping organs instead of two," he said.

A key finding is the date of the fossils: Six distinct techniques converge on an estimated age of roughly 430,000 years old. One technique dated crystals of calcium carbonate that had built up on skulls at the bottom of shallow pools. Another dated the light colored mud that sits atop the red mud in which the fossils are embedded.

This precise dating makes the Sima fossils the oldest in the Neanderthal lineage and confirms that the ancestors of modern humans and the Neanderthal line diverged more than 430,000 years ago.

Arsuaga and his colleagues believe these proto-Neanderthals possessed the power of speech and lived in social groups. The fossils in the Sima pit come from people who lived close to one another in time and were possibly members of a clan, the scientists said.

There are few human ancestors more intriguing than the Neanderthals, who could be described as the best example in the history of the planet of an intelligent species that has gone extinct. They had large craniums, and larger brains than modern humans. They existed as recently as about 30,000 years ago, when their kind disappears from the fossil record.

How they died out, and why, and to what extent they may have interbred with anatomically modern humans, is an ongoing source of debate. Recent research shows some admixture of genes, with modern humans outside of Africa having roughly 1% to 3% Neanderthal DNA.

But as a species, the Neanderthal vanished. In their place came anatomically modern humans, who evolved in Africa and are the ancestors of everyone alive today.

The Neanderthals, Tattersall said, "obviously were very intuitively smart. They were great tool makers. They were ingenious. They were resourceful. They were living through difficult times."

But they did not create symbolic objects, such as artwork, and presumably their speech did not include symbolic language, he said. They may not have imagined the future or created narrations of the past the way we do. Tattersall said the first symbolic objects are geometrical engravings on smooth ochre plaques in southern Africa, dated to about 80,000 years ago.

The new discoveries in [Spain](https://www.theguardian.com/world/spain) add to the mounting evidence that human prehistory was a complicated period with a diverse cast of human species.

"We tend to think it's normal for there to be only one kind of Homo in the world," Tattersall said. "But if you look back on the fossil record, you realize it's totally routine to have several different types of species of Homo in the world, trying to exist at the same time. What is unusual is for us to be on our own. I think that says something very specific about how different we are."

Scientists are redrawing the picture of human evolution in Western Europe.

![Image 1](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/not-quite-neanderthal-300x167.jpg)

They looked something like Neanderthals. But they weren’t classic Neanderthals. Not exactly.

For one thing, they lived 430,000 years ago in what is today northern Spain. Neanderthals have not been traditionally known, at least by the fossil evidence, to have walked the earth at that time. The oldest recovered classic Neanderthal fossil dates to about 200,000 years ago, though many scientists have suggested that Neanderthals lived more anciently, as their distinctive stone tools, known as the [Mousterian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mousterian) industry, have been dated to far earlier times.

Were these humans ancestral to Neanderthals? Possibly so. But the people most familiar with their bones, scientists like Juan Luis Arsuaga of the Centro Mixto Universidad Complutense of Madrid, Spain, are saying that they might have been something else.

_The Bone Studies_

Their bones were excavated by Arsuaga and his team beginning in 1997 within a subterranean chamber created by nature at the terminus of a natural vertical 13-meter subterranean [karstic](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst) shaft. Spelunkers and scientists call it the “chimney”, and for good reason—it’s a bit like negotiating down the interior of a house chimney. Entering the shaft can only be done by traversing through yet another, much larger cave—Cueva Mayor—part of a larger karstic mountain complex in northern Spain called [Atapuerca](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atapuerca_Mountains). Atapuerca is important because here in the caves of these mountains scientists have found fossils and stone tools of some of the earliest known humans in Western Europe, and this small cave at the end of the vertical shaft is arguably the star of the show. Here, over a period of more than two decades, teams of archaeologists and other specialists have excavated over 6,700 human fossils of at least 28 individuals, individuals who lived more than 400,000 years ago. Aptly named [Sima de los Huesos](http://archaeology.about.com/od/lowerpaleolithic/fl/Sima-de-los-Huesos-Spain.htm) (“Sima”), or “Pit of Bones”, it is to date the largest single assembly of early human fossil remains ever found at any single site in the world. The new questions precipitated by the findings at the site have stirred the scholarly world of human evolution. Dating to 430,000 years ago, “this unique collection has to be compared with the much more fragmentary and generally isolated remains yielded by other [Middle Pleistocene](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Pleistocene) sites in Europe and out of Europe,” said Arsuaga. It offered Arsuaga and his team a unique opportunity to study a scene on the stage of the evolution of Middle Pleistocene humans, an unprecedented collection of fossils representing a single population of a [hominin](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hominini) (early human) species.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 2: simapic](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/20410788134_96cd50aeef_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "simapic")

[![Image 3: huesospic2](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/20879025839_79a672dcf5_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "huesospic2")

The paper, by Juan-Luis Arsuaga at Centro Mixto UCM-ISCIII de Evolución y Comportamiento Humanos in Madrid, Spain, and colleagues was titled, ‘Neandertal roots: Cranial and chronological evidence from Sima de los Huesos.’ Image courtesy Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 4: huesospic6](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/20877812740_c9df8f699b_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "huesospic6")

Professor Juan Luis Arsuaga holds one of the many fossil specimens found at the site. This image relates to a paper that appeared in the 20 June, 2014, issue of _Science_, published by AAAS. The paper, by Juan-Luis Arsuaga at Centro Mixto UCM-ISCIII de Evolución y Comportamiento Humanos in Madrid, Spain, and colleagues was titled, ‘Neandertal roots: Cranial and chronological evidence from Sima de los Huesos.’ Image courtesy Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

After excavation, extensive analysis first centered on 17 skulls. Although some of them had been studied before, seven have been presented anew, and six are now more complete than ever before, after many hours of painstaking reconstruction in the lab. With these mostly intact samples for study, the researchers were beginning to more clearly define the common features of this population. Most striking, the examiners found that the fossils exhibited a mosaic of physical characteristics that could not be wholly attributed to any single, recognized human species to date. The skull samples showed clear [Neanderthal](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal) features in the face and teeth. The researchers suggested the ‘Neanderthal-derived’ features were functionally related to mastication, or chewing. “It seems these modifications had to do with an intensive use of the frontal teeth,” Arsuaga said. “The incisors show a great wear as if they had been used as a ‘third hand,” typical of Neanderthals.” But elsewhere, the skulls showed characteristics that diverged from the Neanderthal model. The braincase itself, for example, still showed features associated with more primitive hominins. The crania or skulls were indicating that these were not really Neanderthals\*

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 5: huesospic3](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/21066014605_00e7f90a2b_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "huesospic3")

The paper, by Juan-Luis Arsuaga at Centro Mixto UCM-ISCIII de Evolución y Comportamiento Humanos in Madrid, Spain, and colleagues was titled, ‘Neandertal roots: Cranial and chronological evidence from Sima de los Huesos.’ Image courtesy Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films

The paper, by Juan-Luis Arsuaga at Centro Mixto UCM-ISCIII de Evolución y Comportamiento Humanos in Madrid, Spain, and colleagues was titled, ‘Neandertal roots: Cranial and chronological evidence from Sima de los Huesos.’ Image courtesy Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films

[![Image 7: huesospic5](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/20443631404_a475f810b6_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "huesospic5")

The paper, by Juan-Luis Arsuaga at Centro Mixto UCM-ISCIII de Evolución y Comportamiento Humanos in Madrid, Spain, and colleagues was titled, ‘Neandertal roots: Cranial and chronological evidence from Sima de los Huesos.’ Image courtesy Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Above: A video inside look of the team at work inside the cave. Courtesy Madrid Scientific Films

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Next, the team examined the bones of the postcranial skeletons—all bones other than the skulls. They closely examined and measured 1,523 fossil elements from the collection, representing a minimum number of 19 individuals, using raw values for key skeletal parts as proxies to estimate stature, body breadth, and weight. They also compared the results for the same values from data derived from other early human fossils, including hominins dated to much earlier times. From these results, they were able to characterize the body design of postcranial skeletons, finding that these individuals were relatively tall (by early human standards), with wide, muscular bodies. Although similarly built to Neanderthals, they had generally less brain mass than the classic Neanderthals. They were shorter, wider and more robust than the much later _Homo sapiens_, or modern humans (MH), with less brain to body mass. Like the results of the skull study, the researchers observed that these humans shared many anatomical features with Neanderthals, although some other key Neanderthal features were not present.\*\*

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 8: postcranialpic](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/21041012211_e01f83ca8d_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "postcranialpic")

This image shows the upper and lower limb bones of those adults found in Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca, Spain. Image from Carretero et al.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 9: postcranialpic2](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/21007186956_a45d11aeb4_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "postcranialpic2")

This is a complete Sima skeleton assembled from samples excavated at Sima de los Huesos. Image courtesy Javier Trueba, Madrid Scientific Films

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

So what did these findings mean?

“Morphologically, the Sima de los Huesos skulls \[and postcranial skeleton\] exhibit some (generally incipient) Neanderthal traits,” said Arsuaga. “These traits have been scrutinized to understand how the Neanderthal specializations developed……..and it is now clear that the full suite of Neanderthal characteristics did not evolve at the same pace.” However, according to Arsuaga,”we think based on the morphology that the Sima people were part of the Neanderthal [clade](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clade), although not necessarily direct ancestors to the classic Neanderthals.”

“Not necessarily direct ancestors” was an operative statement, because another study, conducted by Matthias Meyer and a team from the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, indicated a genetic connection of the Sima group to [Denisovans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denisovan), a newly discovered extinct human species that heretofore had been known to exist primarily in Asia at least 40,000 years ago. Those researchers found that the Sima group shared a common ancestor with the Denisovans about 700,000 years ago. “The fact that the [mtDNA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitochondrial_DNA) of the Sima de los Huesos hominin shares a common ancestor with Denisovan rather than Neanderthal mtDNAs is unexpected since its \[the Sima hominin\] skeletal remains carry Neanderthal-derived features”, said Meyer. According to Meyer and colleagues, the age and Neanderthal-like features of the Sima hominins pointed to the possibility that they may have been related to a population ancestral to both Neanderthals and Denisovans. Another possibility, according to Meyers, is that gene flow from a different group of hominins introduced Denisova-like mtDNA into the Sima hominins or their ancestors.\*\*\*

More recent sequencing\[1\] of the nuclear DNA taken from a tooth and leg bone has produced some startling new results, however. As reported by Meyer, the results of that sequencing has suggested that the Sima group was likely more closely related to Neanderthals than they had previously suspected, possibly even as a direct ancestor to Neanderthals. Moreover, the results of the study suggested that the origins of the Neanderthals may need to be pushed significantly back further into time.

Thus, the Sima collection represented an ancestral or sister ancestral group to later Neanderthals, with the findings indicating that the features that distinguished the Neanderthals did not evolve as a single package, but separately in different groups, in a mosaic pattern that eventually came together in the species we know today as classic Neanderthal. The uptake: Human evolution, at least in what is today western Europe, was likely far more complex than the traditional single line paradigm suggested.

_The Million Year Stasis_

But there was another important observation.

By comparing the postcranial fossils to those of other ancient humans, particularly the earlier hominin species that made up the [_Homo_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo) genus (the genus to which Neanderthals and modern humans belong), the researchers also noted that the generally wide Sima skeleton body plan provided additional evidence that early humans, before _Homo sapiens_, changed relatively little in this respect over the one million years preceding the rise of modern humans.

“This is really interesting,” said Binghamton University anthropologist Rolf Quam, a study participant, “since it suggests that the evolutionary process in our genus is largely characterized by stasis (i.e., little to no evolutionary change) in body form for most of our evolutionary history.”

It wasn’t until modern humans, in other words, that humans became taller, narrower, and lighter—along with a greater brain mass to body mass ratio (more [encephalized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encephalization))—a result, some scientists suggest, that reflected evolutionary engineering for greater efficiency, survival and adaptability.

_The Pit of Bones—A Funerary Site?_

So what were the bones of 28 individuals doing in this nearly inaccessible little chamber at the bottom of a difficult-to-negotiate shaft?

It wasn’t an ancient living space. Its size and location, along with the distinct lack of tell-tale evidence of human habitation, precludes this possibility. One thing for sure, however, the skeletal remains represented whole individuals. Although the bones were accompanied by bones of an extinct species of bear, the pattern didn’t indicate that the bone elements were randomly washed down into the cavity from the outside by nature over time or carried into the location by bears or other predators.

Another possible clue came from a recent fascinating finding by another international team of scientists. Led by Nohemi Sala from Centro Mixto UCM-ISCIII de Evolución y Comportamiento Humanos, Spain, this team of researchers examined one particularly peculiar Sima skull (‘Cranium 17’) using modern forensic techniques, including stereoscopic light and digital microscopes, an industrial CT scanner, 3D imaging technology, and contour and trajectory analysis. They focused on two unusual holes or lesions on the frontal bone above the left eye. They were unlike many of the bone fractures on the other bones recovered from the site, which by examination were shown to have been caused by geological process disturbances or as a result of having fallen down a vertical shaft into the cave, perhaps by accident. The results of the study indicated that both fractures were likely produced by two separate impacts by the same object with slightly different trajectories at the same time. According to the researchers, the nature of the lesions indicated that they were likely lethal, and unlikely the result of an accidental fall down the vertical shaft. Rather, the type of fracture, their location, and the appearance of having been produced by two blows with the same object, led the researchers to interpret them as the result of an act of lethal interpersonal aggression. In other words, Sala and his team uncovered what is likely the oldest known case of murder, or violent lethal interpersonal interaction, in human history. Moreover, and most relevant to the interpretation of the site, the study results indicated that the individual was already dead before arrival at the cave site, suggesting that the person was carried to the top of the vertical shaft of the cave and deposited by other humans.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 10: huesospic7](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/21066523405_16bf2c89de_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "huesospic7")

Frontal view of Cranium 17 showing the position of the traumatic events T1 (inferior) and T2 (superior). Courtesy Javier Trueba / Madrid Scientific Films

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 11: huesospic8](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/20445544673_411722a84d_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "huesospic8")

Shown above: The Cranium (Skull) 17 bone traumatic fractures. (A) Frontal view of Cranium 17 showing the position of the traumatic events T1 (inferior) and T2 (superior); (B) Detailed ectocranial view of the traumatic fractures showing the two similar notches (black arrows) present along the superior border of the fracture outlines. Note that the orientation of the two traumatic events is different; (C) Detail of the notch in T1 under 2X magnification with a light microscope. (D) Endocranial view of T1 and T2 showing the large cortical delamination of the inner table (black arrows). From Sala N, Arsuaga JL, Pantoja-Pérez A, Pablos A, Martínez I, Quam RM, et al. (2015) _Lethal Interpersonal Violence in the Middle Pleistocene_. PLoS ONE 10(5): e0126589. doi:10.1371/journal. pone.0126589

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Thus, combined with what scientists already knew about the site and its contents, the finding also led the researchers to another significant conclusion: Given the nature, position, abundance and condition of human bones found within the cave, “the interpretation of the SH site as a place where hominins deposited deceased members of their social groups seems to be the most likely scenario to explain the presence of human bodies at the site,” wrote the study authors in the report. “This interpretation implies this was a social practice among this group of [Middle Pleistocene](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Pleistocene) hominins and may represent the earliest funerary behavior in the human fossil record.”\*\*\*\*

So the Pit of Bones was the prehistoric equivalent of a mass grave or cemetery?

Perhaps, but study of the site and its contents is ongoing. If anything, experience has shown that there may be more surprises to come.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

[![Image 12: huesospic](https://cdn-ilbfgpb.nitrocdn.com/uFIgcGVJNfAaTxVTkPXWYQahoneetLIL/assets/images/optimized/rev-ac577fc/popular-archaeology.com/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/21066709345_b8c5824c5a_z.jpg)](https://popular-archaeology.com/ "huesospic")

Artist’s depiction of the Sima de los Huesos humans. Group picture – no matter what we did, we couldn’t get them to smile. Life was hard 430,000 years ago. Courtesy Javier Trueba, Madrid Scientific Films

\*\*Juan-Luis Arsuaga et al., _Postcranial morphology of the middle Pleistocene humans from Sima de los Huesos,_ Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, [www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.1514828112](http://www.pnas.org/cgi/doi/10.1073/pnas.1514828112)

From the scene, authorities recovered DNA, a stone handaxe and more than 7,000 scattered bones, including a bashed human skull. It was a case for the ages. But there was one complication: the events unfolded 430,000 years ago.

The evidence was unearthed by anthropologists [beginning in the 1980s](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/344/6190/1358.full) at Sima de los Huesos — the “pit of bones” — in Spain’s Atapuerca mountains. The spectacular cave chamber, nearly 100 feet below the surface, has yielded remains from at least 28 hominin individuals. [Ancient DNA analysis](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17405/) of the fossils — the oldest human genetic code ever sequenced — indicates that these people were ancestors to Neanderthals.

After more than three decades of research, the remains have revealed much about Neanderthal evolution. But the circumstances surrounding the group’s death and burial remains contentious. Found in a jumble at the base of a 45-foot chute, some say the bodies were deliberately dropped there after meeting violent ends — a Stone Age cold case.

**Proto-Neanderthals**
----------------------

Since systematic excavations of Sima began in 1984, researchers have discovered thousands of hominin fossils there, but only one artifact: a teardrop shaped handaxe of red and yellow stone, nicknamed Excalibur. There’s more digging to do, though: It’s thought more than half the deposit of sediments and fossils has [yet to be excavated](https://cir.cenieh.es/bitstream/20.500.12136/1203/1/The%20Sima%20de%20los%20Huesos%20origin%20of%20hominin%20accumulation.%20The%20state%20of%20the%20art_Sala_et_al_2018.pdf).

The human remains include at [least 28 individuals](https://www.pnas.org/content/112/37/11524) from both sexes and varying ages. The exact species the Sima individuals belong to is still a topic of debate, but the rich collection has enabled anthropologists to uncover intimate details about their lives as well as their place in the broader story of human evolution.

Compared to modern humans, the Sima humans were short, stocky and smaller-brained. It’s estimated males were about 5 foot 7 and 170 pounds, whereas females stood around 5 foot 2, weighing 125 pounds. Average skull volume was 1230 cm3, about [a half cup less](http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/crux/2018/09/21/neanderthal-brains-bigger-but-not-necessarily-better/#.XXKmu1Bryvt) than Neanderthals (1410 cm3) or modern humans (1350 cm3).

Based on physical appearance, anthropologists have [long argued](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047248497901330) the Sima hominins were [Neanderthal ancestors](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/344/6190/1358.full). The skeletons possess some traits definitive of Neanderthals, which lived about 200,000 years later in Europe. But they lack other classic Neanderthal features, which were yet to evolve.

The proto-Neanderthal hypothesis gained strong support from a [2016 _Nature_ study](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature17405/), which reported DNA from one femur bone and a tooth dated to roughly 430,000 years ago. Although the sequence was just [0.1 percent of a full genome](http://discovermagazine.com/2017/janfeb/4-oldest-human-dna-revises-our-family-tree), it is the oldest hominin DNA ever recovered by nearly 300,000 years. It was also enough to place the Sima humans securely on the evolutionary branch leading to Neanderthals, after it split from the lineage leading to _Homo sapiens_.

**Hidden for a Half Million Years**
-----------------------------------

Today, the Sima chamber sits a quarter-mile’s walk from daylight, deep within a network of caves, which includes other fossil sites between [1000 and 1.2 million years old](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1040618215001512). There may have been shorter routes [430,000 years ago](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/344/6190/1358.full) — when the Sima bones likely accumulated — but researchers studying the cave’s architecture think the only entrance to the chamber itself was the same then as today: a 45-foot vertical chute from a higher level of the cave.

Scientists have proposed a number of hypotheses to explain how the fossils got there. The hominins may have been dragged by carnivores, carried by flood waters or trapped after venturing too far. Meanwhile the excavation team offered a more provocative explanation: The individuals were already dead and intentionally deposited by other humans. This would substantially push back the origin of mortuary practices in human evolution. The earliest well-accepted burials occur only after [130,000 years ago](http://blogs.discovermagazine.com/crux/2018/10/05/human-ancestors-believed-in-the-afterlife/#.XXK7FVBrz5B), among full-fledged Neanderthals and _H. sapiens_.

Over the years analyses have made some of the alternatives [less probable,](https://cir.cenieh.es/bitstream/20.500.12136/1203/1/The%20Sima%20de%20los%20Huesos%20origin%20of%20hominin%20accumulation.%20The%20state%20of%20the%20art_Sala_et_al_2018.pdf) and the “deliberate disposal” hypothesis [more compelling](https://philpapers.org/rec/STILAD). But the matter remains unsettled.

Take the carnivore explanation: In addition to proto-Neanderthals, researchers recovered fossils from more than 175 bears and a smaller number of [other carnivores](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047248497901548), including lions and fox in the cave. However no [typical prey animals](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047248497901536) like mountain goat or deer were found. So was Sima a den for carnivores with an appetite for human meat?

Probably not. No known carnivores — living or extinct — exclusively eat humans. Nor do they make dens _so_ deep in caves. Furthermore, in a [2014](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0277379114001735) [_Quaternary Science Reviews_](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0277379114001735) [study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0277379114001735), researchers scrutinized 2401 human and 1200 carnivore specimens from Sima under the microscope, looking for tooth marks. Just about 4 percent of the human _and_ carnivore bones had bites. This suggests scavengers, at some point, chomped on a small number of these bones, but the site was not a carnivore den.

It seems none of the humans were eaten to death by carnivores. But some may have been beaten to death. According to a [2015](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589) [_PLOS One_](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589) [paper](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0126589), one skull had two fractures, likely caused by a blow from a blunt implement during face-to-face combat. Though not as definitive, [another study](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0305440316300802) the following year identified trauma on eight additional Sima skulls.

It seems to be a convincing case of Stone Age homicide. But that still doesn’t explain how the dead bodies entered the chamber. Were the perpetrators hiding their victims? Or did loved ones inter the corpses, suggesting proto-Neanderthals held beliefs about death and afterlife? That part of the mystery may never be solved.

In any case Sima de los Huesos is one killer pit of bones.

400,000-year-old fossils from Spain provide earliest genetic evidence of Neandertals
====================================================================================

Analysis of nuclear DNA from Sima de los Huesos hominins provides evidence of their relationship to Neandertals

[](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?t=400%2C000-year-old+fossils+from+Spain+provide+earliest+genetic+evidence+of+Neandertals&u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mpg.de%2F10364707%2Fhominins-sima-de-los-huesos "Facebook")[](https://www.linkedin.com/sharing/share-offsite/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mpg.de%2F10364707%2Fhominins-sima-de-los-huesos "LinkedIn")[](https://reddit.com/submit?title=400%2C000-year-old+fossils+from+Spain+provide+earliest+genetic+evidence+of+Neandertals&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mpg.de%2F10364707%2Fhominins-sima-de-los-huesos "Reddit")[](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=400%2C000-year-old+fossils+from+Spain+provide+earliest+genetic+evidence+of+Neandertals&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mpg.de%2F10364707%2Fhominins-sima-de-los-huesos "Twitter")[](whatsapp://send?text=400%2C000-year-old+fossils+from+Spain+provide+earliest+genetic+evidence+of+Neandertals+https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mpg.de%2F10364707%2Fhominins-sima-de-los-huesos "WhatsApp")[](https://www.xing.com/spi/shares/new?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mpg.de%2F10364707%2Fhominins-sima-de-los-huesos "Xing")[](mailto:?body=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.mpg.de%2F10364707%2Fhominins-sima-de-los-huesos&subject=400%2C000-year-old%20fossils%20from%20Spain%20provide%20earliest%20genetic%20evidence%20of%20Neandertals "E-Mail")

March 14, 2016

[Denisovan](https://www.mpg.de/newsroom/Denisovan/en) [Neanderthals](https://www.mpg.de/newsroom/Neanderthals/en)

Previous analyses of the hominins from Sima de los Huesos in 2013 showed that their maternally inherited mitochondrial DNA was distantly related to Denisovans, extinct relatives of Neandertals in Asia. This was unexpected since their skeletal remains carry Neandertal-derived features. Researchers of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, have since worked on sequencing nuclear DNA from fossils from the cave, a challenging task as the extremely old DNA is degraded to very short fragments. The results now show that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were indeed early Neandertals. Neandertals may have acquired different mitochondrial genomes later, perhaps as the result of gene flow from Africa.

![Image 1: The Sima de los Huesos hominins lived approximately 400,000 years ago during the Middle Pleistocene.](https://www.mpg.de/11600542/original-1665066231.jpg?t=eyJ3aWR0aCI6MzQxLCJmaWxlX2V4dGVuc2lvbiI6ImpwZyIsIm9ial9pZCI6MTE2MDA1NDJ9--4ceaf3ac0848b12ec8cca070047dd61831cd6ec9)

![Image 2: The Sima de los Huesos hominins lived approximately 400,000 years ago during the Middle Pleistocene.](https://www.mpg.de/11600542/original-1665066231.jpg?t=eyJ3aWR0aCI6OTY2LCJvYmpfaWQiOjExNjAwNTQyfQ%3D%3D--a446f3de137314162e15043aa19c927f79724015)

The Sima de los Huesos hominins lived approximately 400,000 years ago during the Middle Pleistocene.

© Kennis & Kennis, Madrid Scientific Films

The Sima de los Huesos hominins lived approximately 400,000 years ago during the Middle Pleistocene.

© Kennis & Kennis, Madrid Scientific Films

Until now it has been unclear how the 28 400,000-year-old individuals found at the Sima de los Huesos (“pit of bones”) site in Northern Spain were related to Neandertals and Denisovans who lived until about 40,000 years ago. A previous report based on analyses of mitochondrial DNA from one of the specimens suggested a distant relationship to Denisovans, which is in contrast to other archaeological evidence, including morphological features that the Sima de los Huesos hominins shared with Neandertals.

“Sima de los Huesos is currently the only non-permafrost site that allow us to study DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene, the time period preceding 125,000 years ago”, says Matthias Meyer of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, lead author of an article that was published in Nature today. “The recovery of a small part of the nuclear genome from the Sima de los Huesos hominins is not just the result of our continuous efforts in pushing for more sensitive sample isolation and genome sequencing technologies”, Meyer adds. “This work would have been much more difficult without the special care that was taken during excavation”.

New techniques and precise work make the difference
---------------------------------------------------

![Image 3: Excavation works at the cave site Sima de los Huesos.](https://www.mpg.de/11627353/original-1508158161.jpg?t=eyJ3aWR0aCI6MzQxLCJmaWxlX2V4dGVuc2lvbiI6ImpwZyIsIm9ial9pZCI6MTE2MjczNTN9--e3db26293e02f8e319db4b7fe4ed4c699b6c339f)

![Image 4: Excavation works at the cave site Sima de los Huesos.](https://www.mpg.de/11627353/original-1508158161.jpg?t=eyJ3aWR0aCI6OTY2LCJvYmpfaWQiOjExNjI3MzUzfQ%3D%3D--2de6cfd0abfe11da9a4dabf1845e2388e834ba11)

Excavation works at the cave site Sima de los Huesos.

© Javier Trueba, Madrid Scientific Films

Excavation works at the cave site Sima de los Huesos.

© Javier Trueba, Madrid Scientific Films

“We have hoped for many years that advances in molecular analysis techniques would one day aid our investigation of this unique assembly of fossils”, explains Juan-Luis Arsuaga of the Complutense University in Madrid, Spain, who has led the excavations at Sima de los Huesos for three decades. “We have thus removed some of the specimens with clean instruments and left them embedded in clay to minimize alterations of the material that might take place after excavation.” The nuclear DNA sequences recovered from two specimens secured in this way show that they belong to the Neandertal evolutionary lineage and are more closely related to Neandertals than to Denisovans. This finding indicates that the population divergence between Denisovans and Neandertals had already occurred by 430,000 years ago when the Sima de los Huesos hominins lived.

According to Svante Pääbo of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology “these results provide important anchor points in the timeline of human evolution. They are consistent with a rather early divergence of 550,000 to 750,000 years ago of the modern human lineage from archaic humans”.

Consistent with the previous study, the mitochondrial DNA of the Sima de los Huesos hominins is closer related to Denisovans than Neandertals. Mitochondrial DNA seen in Late Pleistocene Neandertals may thus have been acquired by them later in their history, perhaps as a result of gene flow from Africa. The researchers propose that retrieval of further mitochondrial and nuclear DNA from Middle Pleistocene fossils could help to clarify the evolutionary relationship between Middle and Late Pleistocene hominins in Eurasia.

The Atapuerca system in northern Spain is a unique place for human evolution. In particular, the cave ‘Sima de los Huesos’ is among the sites with the largest number of hominin fossils. For 30 years, more than 7,500 fossils from 29 individuals have been recovered, representing all parts of the skeleton. They are dated to 430,000 years, which makes them the oldest fossils with Neandertal features. All the individuals belong to the same biological population, which is terribly valuable to analyse their variations, sexual differences and patterns of development.

In 2014 the [analysis of the 17 skulls from Sima](http://science.sciencemag.org/content/344/6190/1358) was published. 7 skulls of the collection had not been published before. This study came 21 years after the description of the first 3 skulls.

![Image 1: 17 skulls Sima de los Huesos](https://nutcrackerman.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/17sh.jpg?w=660)

The 17 skulls of Sima de los Huesos. Credit: Javier Trueba, Madrid Scientific Films

### **What are the key conclusions of this study?**

**1)** About the evolution of neandertal features in the Sima materials. Not all the skeleton parts developed simultaneously. The **first neandertal features developed were the teeth**, the jaw and the face, which suggest some masticatory specialization.

**2)** Some **Neandertal traits** are found in the Sima individuals such as:

*   a pronounced brow ridge, not sunk over the nose;
*   the cheeks projected towards the nose, providing a triangular look to the face;
*   the type of engagement of the jaw to the cranium.

**3)** The **braincases are not neandertal-like**. Their average brain size is less than modern humans’ and also less than Neandertals’. The brain evolved quite later.

**4)** The **uniformity of the Sima population** contrasts with the variation when comparing to other European fossils in the Middle Pleistocene (780 to 130,000 years ago). This can be explained by age and regional variations, and also by interbreeding with archaic populations.

This paper followed [another study in 2012 by Chris Stringer](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/227710322_The_status_of_Homo_heidelbergensis_Schoetensack_1908), which helped position the Sima fossils outside the taxon _Homo heidelbergensis_. The Atapuerca team had initially classified the few fossils found in 1993 as _Homo heidelbergensis_, a species described in 1907 with more primitive features than in Sima. Now this is official: they are no longer _Homo heidelbergensis_. But what are they exactly? Early Neandertals, an unknown species ancestor of Neandertal…?

[![Image 2: Cranium 16 Sima de los Huesos Atapuerca](https://nutcrackerman.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/498.jpg?w=300&h=204)](https://nutcrackerman.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/06/498.jpg)

Cranium 16 Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca. Credit: Javier Trueba, Madrid Scientific Films

The amazing collection from Sima de los Huesos will keep growing in the following years – fossils still appear! In 2018 the left side of Cranium 16 was recovered, completing a new skull for this group.

The hominins of Sima de los Huesos are drawing ever closer to the Neanderthals
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Friday, 30 November 2018

he Dental Anthropology Group of the CENIEH has published the first dental histology study of Sima de los Huesos, which reinforces the close relationship between this European Middle Pleistocene population and the species _Homo_ _neanderthalensis_.

![Image 4: Dientes fósiles](https://www.cenieh.es/sites/default/files/styles/max_325x325/public/noticia/images/Nota%20de%20prensa.jpg?itok=ED_CBxUs)

The Dental Anthropology Group of the Centro Nacional de Investigación sobre la Evolución Humana (CENIEH) has just published a paper on dental histology in the journal [Comptes Rendus PALEVOL](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1631068318301076?via%3Dihub), in which a comparison is made for the first time between the sample from the Sima de los Huesos site, in Atapuerca (Burgos), and dental samples from the Neanderthal site of Krapina, in Croatia, as well as with different modern human populations.

This is a comparative study centering on the canines, in which certain dental pieces from Homo antecessor were included, whose results make it clear that the Pleistocene populations at Atapuerca already showed the pattern considered typically Neanderthal in their enamel and dentine volumes.

“The teeth from Sima de los Huesos exhibit large coronal and root dentine dimensions, as well as thin enamel. This histological pattern has traditionally been considered a distinctive trait of the Neanderthals, and it has allowed them to be distinguished both from other groups and from modern humans”, according to Cecilia García Campos, lead author of the paper.

Further, the results of this study might support an early appearance of this highly characteristic dental trait, which had been observed as early as 800,000 years ago in _Homo antecessor_, and maintained in later groups during the Middle Pleistocene.

**Neanderthal lineage**

The fossils found at Sima de los Huesos were initially considered to belong to the taxon _Homo heidelbergensis,_ a species which populated Europe before the Neanderthals, so named from the mandible found in the locality of Heidelberg (Germany).

Nevertheless, a study led by Juan Luis Arsuaga, Centro Mixto UCM-ISCIII de Evolución y Comportamiento Humanos de Madrid, published in 2014 in the journal Science, raised doubts about this assignment, and suggested removing the population at Sima from this taxon because of its evident similarities to _Homo neanderthalensis_.

Later, two genetic studies of Sima de los Huesos, published in the journal _Nature_ in 2014 and 2016, underpinned this decision by showing that these hominins belonged to the Neanderthal evolutionary lineage because of their close relationship to the ancestors of the Neanderthals.

“The dental histology results obtained for the individuals at la Sima de los Huesos support the close relationship there must have been between the Middle Pleistocene hominins at Atapuerca and the later Neanderthal groups living in Europe”, adds García Campos

Posteriormente, dos estudios genéticos de la Sima de los Huesos, publicados en la revista Nature en 2014 y 2016, reforzaban esta decisión demostrando que estos homínidos pertenecían al linaje evolutivo neandertal por su estrecha relación con los antepasados de los neandertales.

“Los resultados obtenidos de la histología dental de los individuos de la Sima de los Huesos apoyan la estrecha relación que debió existir entre los homínidos del Pleistoceno Medio de Atapuerca y los grupos neandertales posteriores que habitaron en Europa”, señala Cecilia García Campos.
